subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 3 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about networks. A network is a group of computers and devices joined together so they can share — share files, share a printer, and send each other messages. You already live inside networks every day: the computers at Ehel Academy that reach the same printer, the Wi-Fi the family's phones join at home, and the internet that carries a message from Hargeisa to Mogadishu are all networks at work. First, a network has two kinds of computer: a server, which gives out services (it stores, finds and sends files, and lets computers share and talk), and a client, which asks the server for what it needs. You meet the file, web, print and mail servers, and see a client send a request and the server send back a response. Second, the difference between the internet (all the world's networks joined together) and the World Wide Web (one service on it: the web pages we open in a browser). Third, that networks can be wired (ethernet cables) or wireless (Wi-Fi, using radio waves), and when each is better.

outcomes: Explain that a network is computers joined together to share files, devices and messages.
Say what a server does and what a client does, and give an example of each.
Name different servers (file, web, print, mail) and match each to its job.
Describe how a client sends a request and a server sends back a response.
Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
Say what a browser, a hyperlink and a website are.
Describe the difference between a wired (ethernet) and a wireless (Wi-Fi) network.

Follow simple rules to help keep a network, and themselves, safe online.

concepts.title: What is a network? Servers and clients
concepts.explanation: A network is computers and devices joined together so they can share — files, a printer, messages. It has two kinds of computer. A server gives out services: it stores, finds and sends files, and lets the other computers share things and talk to one another. A client is a computer that asks the server for what it needs, like a file or a web page. One child is the waiter; the others are customers. Each customer asks for something; the waiter finds it and brings it back. Afterwards ask: what was the waiter's job? (To serve.) The customer's? (To ask.) Then reveal the secret: “On a network the waiter is the server and the customers are the clients — the customer asks, and the server serves.”
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: What is a network? Servers and clients? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Listen for you using the waiter-and-customer picture to explain it.

concepts.title: Meet the servers, and how a request travels
concepts.explanation: A network can have more than one server, each with its own job. A file server stores files for everyone. A web server holds and sends web pages. A print server sends documents to a printer. A mail server passes emails between people. (Others exist too, like an application server for running programs, but these four are the main ones.) Whatever the server, the pattern is the same: the client sends a request, and the server sends back a response. A big restaurant might have one waiter just for drinks, one just for meals, and one just for desserts — each does its own job. A network is the same: different servers for different jobs.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: meet the servers, and how a request travels. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you see that the client always asks first and the server answers, and that the journey goes there (request) and back (response)? Can you match a job to the right server (email to the mail server, printing to the print server)?

concepts.title: The internet and the World Wide Web
concepts.explanation: The internet is a worldwide network of networks — all the world's networks joined together, linking millions of computers, phones and tablets. The World Wide Web is not the same: the Web is just one service on the internet — a huge collection of web pages we open with a browser. Email, video calls and messaging also run on the internet, but are not the Web. A hyperlink jumps you from one web page to another; a group of linked pages is a website. This is the trickiest idea of the unit, so use a picture. The internet is like a huge country with roads joining every town.
concepts.example: The World Wide Web is like all the libraries in that country — wonderful to visit, but only one of the things the roads reach. Email vans and video-call vans use the same roads, but they are not libraries.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you give an example of something on the internet that is not the Web (email, a video call)? Do not worry if this takes time — even adults mix these up.

concepts.title: Wired and wireless: ethernet and Wi-Fi
concepts.explanation: A network can be wired or wireless. A wired network joins its devices with cables — the cables are called ethernet. A wireless network joins its devices through the air using invisible radio waves, and the set of rules the devices use to do this is called Wi-Fi. Each kind is better for different jobs. A wired network is like being joined by a rope — strong, fast and steady, but you cannot walk away. A wireless network is like calling across a room — free to move, but weaker the further you go, and others might overhear. Wired is faster and more secure; wireless lets you move.
concepts.example: Find one real example of wired and wireless: ethernet and Wi-Fi around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Watch for the slip of thinking wireless is simply better; nudge you to weigh speed and safety too.

concepts.title: Be a network designer, and keep it safe
concepts.explanation: A good designer asks: what do we want to share? which computer is the server? which are the clients? and should each device be wired or wireless? At the same time, we keep the network — and ourselves — safe, because a network (especially wireless) can be reached by outsiders if we are not careful. Nadia learnt about networks at Ehel Academy, and wants to help her family join their computer, phones and tablets into one network to share photos and reach the printer. But her family ask: what is a network? who is the server? cables or Wi-Fi?
concepts.example: Do it yourself: be a network designer, and keep it safe. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you make a design choice and give a reason, pick the safe options, and explain why a network needs a password?

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

I can say what a server does and what a client does, and give an example of each.
I can name different servers (file, web, print, mail) and match each to its job.
I can describe how a client sends a request and a server sends back a response.
I can explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
I can say what a browser, a hyperlink and a website are.
I can describe the difference between a wired (ethernet) and a wireless (Wi-Fi) network.
I can choose wired or wireless for a situation and give a reason — being a network designer.
I can follow simple rules to help keep a network, and themselves, safe online.
